concepts.preferred_label: Heart Failure with Reduced Ejection Fraction
concepts.why: Patient has NYHA stage III heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (<25%)
Patient has a history of heart failure
Patient has a history of hypertension
Patient presents with bilateral scrotal and lower extremity edema
Patient has elevated brain natriuretic peptide levels
Patient has global hypokinesis
Patient has a heart rate of 100
Patient has alternating QRS complex morphologies
Patient has alternating QRS complex morphologies
Patient has elevated troponin levels
It explains the bilateral scrotal and lower extremity edema.

rationales.F01: Bilateral scrotal and lower extremity edema is a common symptom of fluid overload, which is often associated with heart failure.
rationales.F06: A left ventricular ejection fraction of less than 25% is a key diagnostic criterion for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.
rationales.F07: Global hypokinesis is a characteristic feature of cardiomyopathy, which can lead to heart failure.
rationales.F08: Sinus tachycardia can be a sign of various conditions, including cardiac arrhythmia and myocardial injury.
rationales.F09: Alternating QRS complex morphologies are a hallmark of Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, a type of cardiac arrhythmia.
rationales.F10: Elevated troponin levels are a marker of myocardial injury.
rationales.F11: High brain natriuretic peptide levels are often seen in patients with heart failure, particularly those with reduced ejection fraction.
rationales.F12: NYHA stage III heart failure with reduced ejection fraction is a specific diagnosis that is strongly associated with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.
